title: Looking Ahead to the Next Generation of Malaria Tools
content:
Malaria kills around 600,000 people annually, most of them young children in Africa. Preventing malaria has long been a focus of GiveWell’s grantmaking, primarily through two proven interventions: insecticide-treated nets, which protect people while they’re sleeping, and seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), which provides preventive antimalarial medicine to young children during the months when malaria transmission is highest.

As our Malaria team has grown and specialized, we’ve been able to expand beyond those two interventions. To make more progress against this disease, we recently announced plans to [further scale our malaria grantmaking](https://blog.givewell.org/2026/10/26/further-scaling-our-malaria-grantmaking/). As part of that effort, we’re funding monitoring and evaluation, as well as other research, to learn more about the effectiveness and potential harms of newer strategies for preventing and treating malaria. This work will help us prepare to fund the scale-up of promising and cost-effective programs in the years ahead.

In this [episode](https://givewell.transistor.fm/episodes/looking-ahead-to-the-next-generation-of-malaria-tools), GiveWell co-founder and CEO Elie Hassenfeld speaks with three members of our Malaria research team—Senior Researcher James Watson, Senior Researcher Lucy McNamara, and Senior Program Officer Rosie Bettle—about new tools that could help prevent or treat malaria in the future.

Elie, James, Lucy, and Rosie discuss:

*   **Building evidence on spatial emanators:** Spatial emanators are small plastic sheets hung inside homes that release insecticide to repel and kill mosquitoes. Unlike insecticide-treated nets, which protect people as they sleep, spatial emanators protect people whenever they’re indoors. While there are a number of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of spatial emanators, only two trials assessing the ability of these devices to prevent malaria took place in Africa, where malaria burden is highest. One, conducted in Kenya, found that they reduced malaria infections by about one-third; the other, in Mali, found no effect, though that trial faced some challenges and was unable to achieve high coverage. We’re funding monitoring and evaluation of pilot implementation of spatial emanators alongside nets in Burkina Faso, Sierra Leone, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to learn more about their effectiveness, how many people they reach, and whether they impact net use. If the evidence holds up, emanators could be a highly cost-effective way to protect people, including where living situations make it harder to hang sleeping nets. 
*   **Speeding up research on insecticide-treated baby wraps:** In many African countries, mothers carry infants and young children on their backs in cloth wraps. Treating the wraps with insecticide could provide protection from mosquito bites during a period when children are particularly vulnerable to die from malaria. An RCT in Uganda found that wraps treated with permethrin, an insecticide extensively used to treat bed nets, reduced malaria illness by about two-thirds. However, in this trial the baby wraps were retreated every month, and real-world settings are unlikely to achieve this level of adherence. Long-lasting factory-treated wraps are a more promising option, so we recently funded a trial in DRC of two insecticides for factory-treated wraps designed to last for up to a year. Positive results could support a change in World Health Organization guidance and lead to broader adoption. 
*   **Exploring other tools at earlier stages:** We’re looking at several different tools in earlier stages of development or which have not yet been widely adopted. Malaria gene drives are one of these tools. They genetically modify mosquitoes so they’re less likely to transmit malaria—such as by reducing fertility to reduce the overall mosquito population. To facilitate the future rollout of gene drives, we’re exploring opportunities to strengthen countries’ capacity to evaluate the potential use of gene drives and helping communities get accurate information. Antimalarial suppositories are another tool in an earlier stage. Children with severe malaria who are too sick to swallow pills currently have to travel to a hospital to receive injections or IV treatment, delaying life-saving treatment. Community health workers could provide treatment more quickly with antimalarial suppositories, but they have not yet been widely adopted. We’re considering ways to strengthen community health worker systems to improve access to treatment for malaria and other childhood illnesses, which would reduce geographic and financial barriers to care. 

Each of these tools could expand the range of highly cost-effective malaria programs we’re able to fund in the years ahead, but some are still far from being delivered at scale. Alongside our continued support for proven programs like nets and SMC, we are working to better understand the evidence for new tools and their cost-effectiveness, alongside their potential harms and barriers to delivery. With this information, we will be better positioned to direct donors’ funds to the programs where we believe they can do the most good.

Read more about [how our malaria research is growing](https://blog.givewell.org/2026/05/28/growing-givewells-largest-research-area-malaria/). Visit our [All Grants Fund](https://www.givewell.org/all-grants-fund) page to learn more about how you can support this work, and listen or [subscribe to our podcast](https://givewell.transistor.fm/subscribe) for our latest updates.

_This episode was recorded on November 13, 2026, and represents our best understanding at that time._

title: Messing with the thermostat
content:
No matter how high you turn the thermostat, your house will take just as long to get to 72 degrees.

Second metaphor: You can’t make a pizza faster in a 2,000 degree oven. In fact, you’ll incinerate it, not cook it.

Third metaphor: Two people can have one conversation and meet each other. For a group of 11, it’s 55 conversations.

Fourth metaphor: It’s easier to salt bland food at the table than to fix over-salted food in the kitchen.

title: A Physician Explains GLP-1s’ Biggest Potential Side Effect: A Rare But Serious Eye Condition
content:
GLP-1 drugs must now carry a warning label about a [potential link to a rare eye condition](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential) that can result in vision loss, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced on November 9, 2026. The eye condition is called [non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy](https://www.aao.org/eyenet/article/naion-diagnosis-and-management), or NAION, and doctors often refer to it as a [stroke](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/5601-stroke) of the eye.

I am a [clinician and epidemiologist](https://ziyadalaly.com/) who has studied GLP-1 drugs, and my colleagues and I published one of the studies that identified a [link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.9917).

Millions of people around the world take these medications—including [30 million in the U.S.](https://news.gallup.com/poll/712157/glp-usage-reaches-new-high.aspx)—to [treat diabetes and obesity](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK551568/) and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. They are also being investigated for an [expanding list of clinical conditions](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-024-03412-w).

The data on which the FDA’s warning is based suggests a real but low risk of NAION for people taking GLP-1 medications. This is not a trivial or inconsequential outcome for those who develop the eye stroke. But on balance, if you’re using the medication for an FDA-approved condition such as diabetes or obesity on the advice of your doctor, the risk should not deter you from doing so.

Here’s what patients who use GLP-1 drugs need to know about this rare but serious side effect.

**What is NAION?**

NAION is an injury to the [optic nerve](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/22261-optic-nerve), which is the nerve that connects the eye to the brain. This eye condition is caused by a sudden reduction in blood flow. Without enough blood flow, patients may experience sudden, painless blurry vision, dark patches, partial loss of vision or even blindness.

These symptoms generally persist and often lead to permanent visual impairment. Patients often notice these symptoms first thing in the morning when they wake up, as it tends to happen more frequently at night when blood pressure is naturally lower.

[Video 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fQVq8mtsVog)

**How Did the FDA Identify the Connection?**

As use of GLP-1 drugs increased—particularly since [2021, when they were approved for obesity](https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/952441)—cases of NAION began to emerge. A 2024 study of close to 17,000 patients referred to ophthalmology clinics was the first to show a potential link. It reported [an increased risk of the eye condition](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2024.2296) among the subset of those patients who were prescribed a GLP-1 drug.

To determine that the connection was strong enough to merit a warning, the [FDA first compiled data](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-communications/fda-requires-safety-labeling-changes-glucagon-peptide-1-receptor-agonists-glp-1-ras-due-potential) from 126 randomized, controlled clinical trials of GLP-1 drugs. Those trials included a total of 134,253 patients—78,217 of them were on GLP-1 drugs and 56,036 received a placebo or a different medication, for comparison.

Per year, on average, the incidence of NAION cases was 6.4 per 100,000 people for patients taking the GLP-1 drugs and 3.8 per 100,000 among people given a placebo or other drug. This translated into 2.6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients on GLP-1 drugs.

In a separate analysis, the FDA reviewed GLP-1 drug data from its own network of [sentinel programs](https://www.fda.gov/safety/fdas-sentinel-initiative) that track the real-world safety of approved medications. They assessed how often people with type 2 diabetes who started either a GLP-1 drug or two other common types of diabetes medications reported having NAION between 2019 and 2024.

Patients taking GLP-1 drugs had a small but meaningfully higher risk compared to one type of diabetes drug, called DPP-4 inhibitors, which prevent the breakdown of the body’s own natural GLP-1. Over the course of one year, those taking GLP-1 drugs experienced NAION at a rate of 32 per 100,000 and those taking DPP-4 inhibitors at a rate of 26 per 100,000. This resulted in 6 extra cases of NAION per 100,000 patients among people on GLP-1 drugs.

**Is There Other Evidence of the Risk?**

Other studies that use real-world data such as electronic health records or insurance claims to track the health of people over many years have also found a consistent [association between GLP-1 drugs and NAION](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc25-1238).

For example, my colleagues and I tracked nearly [600,000 U.S. veterans with type 2 diabetes](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.9917) starting either a GLP-1 drug or a different drug over three years. For patients on GLP-1 drugs, we found that the incidence of this eye disorder was roughly 390 cases per 100,000 people, compared with 290 per 100,000 on an alternative medication. In other words, among people taking GLP-1 drugs, there were about 100 extra cases per 100,000 patients.

That number varied somewhat across studies, probably because of group differences among patients. For example, in some, patients were on average older, or also had other conditions that might contribute to their risk.

What’s clear is that the slightly increased risk of NAION does not seem to be specific to any one GLP-1 drug but can occur regardless of which GLP-1 drug a patient takes. It’s possible that some GLP-1 drugs may have a higher risk than others, but so far, there’s no research addressing this.

The FDA’s announcement follows a 2025 review by European regulators, which examined NAION risk in only one type of GLP-1 drug, called semaglutide. It concluded that this eye condition is a [very rare side effect of semaglutide](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/news/prac-concludes-eye-condition-naion-very-rare-side-effect-semaglutide-medicines-ozempic-rybelsus-wegovy) and mandated that the package insert be updated to include NAION as a very rare side effect.

**The Upshot for Patients**

The risk of NAION with GLP-1 drugs is likely real. All the evidence—the FDA’s two analyses, the real-world studies conducted by independent researchers and the fact that two regulators reached the same view independently—points in the same direction.

But in terms of the total number of people who are likely to experience this side effect, the risk is small. In my view, this makes the FDA’s warning not a cause for alarm but rather an unlikely but not impossible outcome that both clinicians and patients should be aware of.

Clinicians should discuss it with their patients before prescribing a GLP-1 drug—and patients should be educated on the symptoms of NAION and how to tell if they are experiencing it.

Patients should also seek immediate care at the earliest signs of vision problems. For patients who have previously had NAION or who already have [risk factors for it](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2021.618353), including smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, anemia and kidney disease, careful discussion weighing the risks and benefits is important. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: What Do Peahens Really Want?
content:
First of all, there was the trick of staying submerged long enough to hear him. My 3-millimeter wetsuit was made of neoprene, a rubber infused with tiny gas bubbles, and I felt as buoyant as a cork. I was off the coast of Mo’orea, a small island in French Polynesia, floating on the deep cerulean-blue sea.

I could just make him out in the distance: the faint white outline of pectoral fins and underbelly, a ghostly silhouette of a male humpback whale suspended vertically, nose pointing down to the ocean floor. He was a giant school bus of a creature dwarfed only by the ocean itself, yet whose song commanded the great expanse. His plaintive chant—ascending high notes interrupted with bass staccatos that caused my flippers to vibrate—was amplified by the walls of the barrier reef. I was getting cold, but the pleasure of his song overpowered my numbing limbs. I wanted to keep myself in the presence of beauty for just a moment longer.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from _Nautilus_.  
To get it in print, **[join by Nov 30](https://nautil.us/hotissue?utm_source=beehiiv&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=issuerelease-issue69-t1-202611&utm_term=free)**.

Beauty. Did other whales off the coast of Mo’orea hear beauty in the song? Do other animals sense beauty?

None other than Charles Darwin thought so. He believed animals got pleasure from admiring shapes, colors, patterns, and sounds. On visits to the Zoological Gardens in London, he enjoyed the peacocks’ decorated, iridescent plumes, and imagined that the peahens admired the peacock’s tail “as much as we do.” Birds weren’t the only nonhuman aesthetes. Darwin thought spiders had an eye for beauty, too. He mused that since we evolved from a common ancestor, it’s possible that much more life on Earth could have a “taste for the beautiful.”

Yet the biological processes for how this might work remained a mystery to him. In _On the Origin of Species_, published in 1859, Darwin circled the riddle of how life evolved from a common ancestor through natural selection, and later, in _The Descent of Man_, he was concerned with the nature of animals’ sense of beauty. The first was solved a century later with the discovery of genetic inheritance through DNA. The second riddle is still an open question.

Most scientists after Darwin—biologists especially—dropped the question entirely. Victorians didn’t like the idea that the appreciation of beauty, often considered evidence of the soul, could be shared with beasts. There was also growing consensus among scientists that nonhuman animal traits and behaviors could be explained through the evolutionary goals of sex, food, and shelter alone. Even now it’s met with suspicion. Beauty, the assumption goes, is in the eye of the beholder, who can only be human.

But modern evolutionary biologists have gathered evidence that animals from baboons to birds, honeybees to fish, might have a sense of beauty. As squishy as that might sound, a large body of research in psychology, neurobiology, and computational neuroscience treats beauty as an empirical phenomenon that can be defined and tested. Although most of this research focuses on humans, scientists believe there are strong parallels that can be drawn to nonhuman animals.

Tamra Mendelson, a professor of evolutionary biology and behavioral ecology at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, is a leader in the field. She’s heard all the criticisms of her work being anthropomorphic. One day, after she gave a talk proposing that nonhuman animals share brain processes with us that correlate with experiencing beauty, a colleague walked up to her and said, “You know, this is all really great but just drop the beauty part.”

“I’m not going to drop it,” Mendelson said to me recently with a warm laugh. “Beauty is real. It’s a real experience. You have it. He has it. We’re all animals, and we have it.”

In what ways, though, do animals sense beauty? What role does it play in mating, in adaptation and evolution? Mendelson and her colleagues answer those questions and boldly propose that beauty is its “own self-sufficient source of pleasure,” as they write in a 2025 paper, “On the biological basis of beauty.” We’re not the only ones on this planet to enjoy something simply for its beauty. Animals too might experience beauty for beauty’s sake.

**DARTING BEAUTY:** The extraordinary color patterns of darter fish cannot be explained simply as camouflage from predators or mating signals. _CREDIT: Dhester88 / Wikimedia Commons_

Mendelson didn’t study beauty at the outset of her scientific career. She was struck by it instead. While a graduate student at Duke University, she had a stint between 1993 and 1994 studying lemurs at the Duke Lemur Center, where she found herself chasing after the primates in the cold to record whether the dominant female gets to be the warmest by being in the middle of the huddle.

Her luck changed when a mentor handed her a bunch of papers on darters, a fish species native to North America found in the shallows of streams and lakes. Mendelson knew she’d found her ideal candidate. Darters could be studied in a laboratory aquarium that recreates their natural habitat, and she could watch them while seated with a cup of coffee. That wasn’t the only perk. It was also their looks. “I can’t stand it, they’re so beautiful,” she said.

During breeding season, male darters, such as the candy darter of West Virginia, are so brilliantly colored and strikingly patterned that it’s hard to peel your eyes away. Even on a computer screen they’re mesmerizing: Their bellies are splashed with red encircled in gold, their tails and backs are painted with shimmery turquoise, and their dorsal fins alternate vibrant orange and blue. The darter was Mendelson’s peacock. And just like Darwin, a question hovered in Mendelson’s mind: Why do they look like this? “I studied the role of mate choice in speciation, and nothing made sense,” she said.

Mendelson was skeptical that the males’ coloring and patterning served as camouflage to blend into the environment and hide them from predators. Their resplendence made the animals more, not less, detectable by predators. The camouflage angle similarly failed to explain why the females weren’t colored like the males. Wouldn’t they need camouflage protection the most? They are the ones with the eggs, after all, and getting gobbled up would put the species at risk.

Mendelson also wasn’t persuaded that the decorative features merely signaled “good genes”—also the conventional explanation for the peacock’s plumage. The good genes theory goes that an immense and brilliant display of tail feathers takes a lot of metabolic energy to build and maintain, and a weak or sick male would not be able to both subsist and have fantastic feathering. In short, the more prodigious the plumage, the healthier the male and the greater chance his offspring will be healthy, too. Yet if these features were only signals of the males’ genetic fitness, then we should expect them to be more like “car alarms and stop signs,” Mendelson said. Detectable but not ornate.

Mendelson was intrigued by evolutionary biologist Richard Prum’s argument that an appreciation of beauty was involved in animals’ mate selection, and she “liked the idea of an aesthetic sense.” But his theory didn’t go far enough. Prum, she said, “doesn’t offer any explanation for the particular design of a signal.” It doesn’t explain why a fin or feather is ornately patterned in the way it is. At this point in her career, Mendelson recalled, she remained “baffled by the designs.”

**BIOLOGIST IN THE HOUSE:** Tamra Mendelson knows she can be seen as trespassing in philosophy by studying beauty. But as an evolutionary biologist, she said, "I can help us understand beauty in a totally different way.” _CREDIT: Photo Courtesy of Tamra Mendelson_

But this changed one summer day in Anchorage in 2015. Mendelson was at the University of Alaska for the annual meeting of the Animal Behavior Society, and attended a talk by Julien Renoult, an evolutionary biologist and cognitive scientist at the French National Center for Scientific Research.

Renoult began his career as a behavioral ecologist studying the fruit of fig trees in Madagascar. During his fieldwork, he noticed how certain birds and monkeys were drawn to the brilliantly colored green, orange, purple, and red fruits. He wondered why color and patterns might attract animals. When he looked for answers, he only came across studies on humans. “In nonhuman animals we had nothing,” Renoult said.

In 2012, Renoult joined a lab in Paris that specialized in the history and philosophy of aesthetics. He spent the next three years poring through the literature on humans’ taste for beauty, while brainstorming how it could be tested in animals. “People thought I was doing strange things,” he said, but “this is something that we can study with a classic scientific approach.”

He came away from his time at that lab with a significant insight—one that he believed helped link ornaments and mate choice in animals, and one in which animal appreciation of beauty is key. But how can you possibly crawl into the mind of another species, such as a peahen, to know whether she has a deeper appreciation for the peacock’s brilliant patterning and not just his sex appeal? You do it indirectly, and Renoult devised a clever hack.

Renoult and his team trained a computer algorithm to process photos of landscapes—forests and sweeping countryside scenes—the way that a human retina and visual cortex would.

Neuroscientists have long known that brains compress information into fewer neurons to save energy, a phenomenon called “efficient processing.” It would cost us too much energy and time to have a neuron fire for each distinct feature of a habitat. Instead, we have specialized neurons that code for patterns in nature such as verticality, symmetry, and roundness. Over time, our brains become tuned to these patterns in our environment. It’s a shortcut that helps us quickly determine whether a place is familiar and safe. It’s also a bias our brains have for these features, and it looks for them everywhere.

The researchers then fed the algorithm photos of women, and had it process their faces using the same vocabulary it built from processing the landscapes. Renoult noticed that some of these faces were processed quickly by the algorithm, requiring very little code. Since the algorithm is a simulation for how our brain works, this finding suggests that our brains encode landscapes and faces in a similar way.

Next, Renoult asked a group of 169 men to rate the same photos of women on a scale of 1 to 20 on attractiveness. He predicted that the more efficiently the algorithm processed a face, the higher the men would rate that face’s attractiveness. He was right. This indicated that “beauty is determined by a particular way of processing information,” he said. Beauty is not a property of an object, but rather the result of an activity in the brain.

Renoult’s study also suggested we find certain faces attractive because they share features with landscapes. Our visual cortex is ancient and evolved to help our forebears’ brains find patterns in their environment. And we are not the only animals with visual cortices that process information in an efficient manner. This compression can emerge and spread through a population over evolutionary time from repeated exposures to the environment, becoming encoded into the genome. Scientists have observed this coding “in all animals, even in invertebrates,” Renoult noted. It’s possible that snails are aesthetes.

While Renoult shared these ideas in the 2015 talk in Alaska, it dawned on Mendelson that she now had a hypothesis she could test. Maybe one reason the female darters were attracted to male darters wasn’t only because they found them arousing, but because their patterning resembled the environment that their brains had adapted to. Maybe attraction between mates in the animal world isn’t always about sex.

**STAR POWER:** Striking regularity in an animal pattern, like the star-shape tail of the greater sage grouse, can trigger pleasure. _CREDIT: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service_

Mendelson and Renoult have found a basis for their theory in many fields, notably neuroaesthetics, the interdisciplinary field that locates our experiences of the arts in the brain. “We’ve evolved from common ancestors, so a lot of our brain architecture is similar,” Mendelson said. Added Renoult, “Everything that characterizes a judgment of beauty in humans—the machinery at least—is present in nonhuman animals.”

With the use of brain scans, scientists studying neuroaesthetics in 2023 reported that when we say something is beautiful, a region deep in our midbrain, the mesolimbic system, generates a feeling of pleasure. Given we share the same basic neural machinery with all vertebrates, studies have shown that some insects, including bees, might have a similar reward system.

The pleasure of beauty is linked to processing information with ease, the same activity in the brain that Renoult discussed in his 2015 talk. Psychologists refer to the pleasure of information-processing as “fluency,” which they equate with beauty. This fluency, inherited from our evolutionary past (coded into our genome) and individual life experiences, can explain why there seems to be some universal qualities that characterize beautiful things, like symmetry.

It also explains why there might be shared aesthetic preferences across species.

A study published this year investigated whether our taste in sounds overlaps with other species’ aural affinities. Turns out, we have the same appreciation for male frog songs that female frogs do. The lower-frequency calls embellished with “trills,” “clicks,” and “chucks” thrill us all, as does the female crickets’ preference for classic “chirps” over “purrs.” We also appear to have similar visual preferences with other species. A 2023 study suggested that jumping spiders like abstract images that contain similar spatial statistics, such as the changes in light and dark across an image, found in natural scenes that we like.

Another key point of Mendelson’s and Renoult’s thesis is that beauty is “disinterested.” When you experience beauty, you’re not concerned about what it’s going to give you beyond the immediate pleasure of appreciating it. The moment you begin to think about what you want, you’ve slipped into desire. Psychologists distinguish the two states as “liking” and “wanting.” Liking is linked with calming neurotransmitters, such as opioids and endocannabinoids; wanting is associated with arousal and dopamine.

But if the experience of beauty isn’t goal-oriented, then it seems irrelevant to the purpose of survival. To put it another way: How does beauty make any evolutionary sense?

The experience of beauty is an adaptive trait, Mendelson explained, but not necessarily for sexual purposes: “The whole process evolved in a different context than sexual communication.” That context is the environment.

Because our brain rewards us with pleasure when we discover patterns and regularities in our surroundings, we are encouraged to continue gathering information. And because our brains are biased toward these patterns, we will find beauty in places unrelated to survival—like on a museum wall or the red carpet. An animal’s experience of ornamental beauty, Mendelson said, is an aesthetic experience not unlike our own, which doesn’t have to involve sexual selection.

Not that beauty has nothing to do with sex. Mendelson explained that beauty can indeed be part of the mating ritual. Although a sense of beauty evolved independently of sex selection, her hypothesis is that it’s “being exploited by sexual actors.” The female darter selects a male whose patterns are as pleasurable to process as those in her environment. Although liking and wanting have different functions, they’re not mutually exclusive. The stunning qualities of a male peacock’s tail give the peahen another reason to stick around, even if she hasn’t made up her mind whether he is boyfriend material.

**KEY OF LIFE:** Turns out, humans have the same appreciation for male frog songs that female frogs do. We get the same thrills. CREDIT: Macropixel / Envato

Innes Cuthill is a behavioral ecologist at the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom who studies adaptive traits in animals, notably coloration. He agrees with Mendelson and Renoult—and Darwin—that human traits can be a guide to understanding animals. “I’m certainly with Darwin in seeing that there’s continuity in emotional states, as well as physical processing and physiology, between other animals and us,” Cuthill said. “I mean, it would be very strange if there wasn’t continuity.”

But Cuthill worries comparing our experience of beauty to animals’ is a step too far. “I don’t necessarily accept that animals are experiencing emotions in the same way as us, and it’s probably impossible, really, to have any sort of subjective understanding of how that might feel,” he said.

Cuthill also questions Renoult’s and Mendelson’s theory that an efficient use of brain energy necessarily connotes pleasure, which leads to an adaptive trait. It’s a jump from measuring an animal’s physiological response, he said, “to saying, ‘Ah, that’s why peacocks have evolved beautiful tails.’” Cuthill doesn’t question the veracity of an experiment showing animals can be either calmed or aroused. He challenges whether the experiment proves attraction. “It doesn’t tell us where the positive axis is, that something should be attractive,” he said.

Currently, Mendelson and Renoult are embarked on a new experiment. They plan to expose female darters to silhouettes of darters with a series of features similar to the environment to see which the fish spend more time actively observing. Their hypothesis remains: Should the fish prefer the images with similar properties to landscapes and endocannabinoids flood their brains, that provides evidence that an animal can exhibit the behavior and biochemical signatures of appreciating beauty.

This past June, Mendelson and Renoult joined an international group of biologists, neuroscientists, philosophers, and artists at the University of Antwerp to discuss LUCAE, “the last universal common aesthetic experience.” It’s a term Jan Verpooten, a research manager at the Antwerp Research Institute for the Arts and the group’s organizer, coined as a play on LUCA—“last universal common ancestor”—the holy grail of evolutionary biologists.

Verpooten, a double doctorate in biology and philosophy, brought the group together to explore the deepest hint of aesthetic capacity in the tree of life. To his mind, it exists among the Bilateria—animals with a central axis and left and right symmetry who have neural processing and seem to experience pleasure. We’re among the Bilateria, but so are worms. So are 99 percent of animal species on Earth today.

If the biologists are right that a taste for beauty isn’t exclusive to humans, that most creatures experience it—it feels like a radically new way to see life on Earth. Like all great de-centerings, there is that moment of awe. We are among the 20 quintillion individual beings alive right now who at any given moment might be taking in something they find wondrous, and I can’t help but think: Isn’t that beautiful? ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: A Rope Bridge Camera Just Discovered a New Species of Howler Monkey
content:
Camera traps are important devices for conservationists and photographers, providing a non-invasive way in which they can keep tabs on the behaviors and movements of wildlife over time. Occasionally, camera traps also help to identify a new species too.

Case in point: A camera trap embedded in the Alta Floresta region of the Amazon rainforest, toward the western edge of Brazil, snapped a photo of a new howler monkey species, _Alouatta matogrossensis_, not long after the species was first described [in a study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-026-11187-8) in _Communications Biology_.

**Read more: “**[**Qatari Sand Cats Caught on Camera for the First Time**](https://nautil.us/qatari-sand-cats-caught-on-camera-for-the-first-time-1282149)**”**

Conservationists set up the trap on the end of a rope bridge installed to keep forested areas connected for tree-dwelling animals. Such bridges enable them to safely cross roads and prevent populations from declining through isolation. “We were all amazed that we were providing safe crossing opportunities for a new monkey species,” Fernanda Abra, a road ecologist who leads [Projecto Reconecta](https://projetoreconecta.com/), told [_National Geographic_](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/new-monkey-species-discovered).

The newly described species Alouatta matogrossensis. _Credit: Bruno Rennó_

As is often the case when a new species is discovered, this type of howler monkey is under threat from several environmental pressures. If it wasn’t, experts likely would have come across it earlier.

In fact, _A. matogrossensis_ has been hiding in plain sight. Previously, researchers had filed it away as being a more common Purus red howler (_Alouatta puruensis_). The fresh analysis of its genetic and physical characteristics revealed the distinction. The team behind the new study thinks _A. matogrossensis_ may have been around for some 500,000 years, contained by rivers on one side of their natural habitat, and by a tropical savanna on the other.

According [to study author Jean Boubli](https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/article/new-monkey-species-discovered), from the University of Salford in the U.K., this patch of ecosystem is “where the forest is at its worst shape in the whole of Brazil.” Deforestation related to agriculture and urbanization has left smaller and smaller areas for these animals to live, even without considering the threat from road vehicle collisions.

With new rope bridges and camera traps—as well as a better understanding of the species that live in this part of the world—conservationists now have a better chance of helping the howler monkey population to grow—and discovering even more species before it’s too late. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Future Lunar Colonists Can Farm Potatoes on the Moon
content:
In the movie _The Martian_, Matt Damon’s character (botanist Mark Watney) finds himself stranded on Mars. With any rescue months away and food supplies dwindling, he decides to do what he does best—grow some plants. Watley mixes the Martian soil with fertilizer provided by the crew’s waste and plants potatoes.

It’s a good plan (spoiler alert: it worked). Potatoes are both nutritionally dense and provide a high number of calories per unit of land (they’re also versatile and delicious). According to a new study [published](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41526-026-00668-z) in _npj Microgravity_, they may even be able to feed future lunar colonists.

**Read more: “[How Potatoes Shaped the Genes of the First People to Grow Them](https://nautil.us/how-potatoes-shaped-the-genes-of-the-first-people-to-grow-them-1280533)”**

To establish a baseline for best lunar farming practices, a team of botanists from Oregon State University relied on simulated moon soil, or regolith. Unlike the living soil here on Earth, moon dirt isn’t exactly conducive to plant growth—it’s nutrient-poor and contains higher levels of toxic heavy metals. So to give the regolith a little boost, they mixed it with various amounts of vermicompost (an organic fertilizer produced by red wiggler worms) as well as additional nitrogen.

The team tested five varieties of simulated lunar soil, some that mimicked low-lying lunar mares and some that mimicked the highlands. As a control, they used soil from Hermiston, Oregon, which has one of the highest yields of potatoes globally (there goes your reputation, Idaho).

The team found that the optimum mix was 30 percent vermicompost and 70 percent regolith. Potatoes grown in this soil were the best match for those grown in good ol’ Hermiston, Oregon dirt. Lower levels of the fertilizer (5 to 15 percent) yielded stunted tubers, dwarfed leaves, and shriveled roots. (Which region of the moon the regolith simulated—highland versus lowland didn’t seem to make much of a difference.)

Looking at the chemical composition of the potatoes, the researchers found they were nutritionally similar to those grown on Earth. In fact, the vermicompost seems to have provided some protection against heavy metals like copper in the regolith.

“We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” study author Aymeric Goyer said in a [statement](https://news.oregonstate.edu/news/study-finds-potatoes-grown-simulated-lunar-soil-match-earth-grown-performance). “That’s an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”

Of course, these findings mean future lunar farmers will have to bring vermicompost or something like it to kick-start their agricultural project. But once they get started, they can resupply using their own organic material. After all, as the fictional Mark Watney discovered, astronauts make pretty good fertilizer producers. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How Our Eyes Betray Us When We Lie
content:
“It takes two to lie: one to lie and one to listen,” isn’t just a famous quote from Homer Simpson, it’s also the spirit of an actual experiment from a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0361498) in _PLOS One_. Psychologists from Ulm University in Germany recently investigated how our eyes react when we’re trying to deceive another actual person.

Here’s how they arranged the experiment: We’ll call our protagonist “Participant” and their partner “Mentalist” (because that’s what they called them in the study. During the investigation this pair sat facing one another at a table. Participant first selected a card with a number from one to six (if it’s important to your mental image, they resembled Uno cards). A screen visible to both Participant and Mentalist then showed the cards in sequence for five seconds each. Afterwards, Mentalist got to ask Participant some yes or no questions (i.e., “Is your card even?”) to try to determine which card they picked.

**Read more: “[The Galaxies in Your Eyes](https://nautil.us/the-galaxies-in-your-eyes-748943)”**

It sounds straightforward, but this is where the lying comes in. Before the sessions, Participant was tasked with either revealing the card to Mentalist, concealing their selection (making sure Mentalist didn’t guess correctly), or faking them out (placing suspicion on another card altogether). Participant was instructed to use nonverbal communication and tailor their question responses to achieve whatever goal they were given. During this little battle of wits, Participant’s eyes were tracked with specialized glasses.

So what did they find?

According to data from 36 participants, our eyes betray us. Regardless of whether the participants were trying to reveal, conceal, or fake out the mentalist, their pupils dilated more when their own card popped up on the screen.

Additionally, when participants tried to conceal the identity of their cards, their gazes showed subtle differences. They blinked less and also showed fewer fixations, but for longer durations (0.9 versus 1.2 seconds). The researchers said this was likely a result of arousal inhibition, or a conscious attempt to suppress reactions. Finally, during the verbal portion, the eyes stopped being so instructive. Instead, the response time seemed to give the concealers and fakers away—truthful responses came a full second quicker than lies.

Of course, the study wasn’t designed to determine the effectiveness of the lies, just how people react physiologically when they’re telling them. Still, it seems like meeting someone’s gaze is as effective a tactic as any for sussing out dishonesty. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: An Epidemiologist Explains What It Will Take for the U.S. to Regain Its Measles Elimination Status
content:
The United States has [lost its measles elimination status](https://kffhealthnews.org/public-health/us-measles-elimination-status-lost-outbreaks-continuous-spread-year-paho-cdc/) – an international designation reflecting an absence of [local measles transmission](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WER9243) for at least 12 months – a public health achievement held [since 2000](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html). A commission of the Pan American Health Organization, a regional office of the World Health Organization that oversees the Americas, reached that conclusion in November 2026, with a [formal announcement expected Nov. 17](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/measles/2-more-people-die-measles-complications-us-cases-top-5400).

Canada lost its measles elimination status [in 2025](https://theconversation.com/canada-loses-its-official-measles-free-status-and-the-us-will-follow-soon-as-vaccination-rates-fall-269090), as did the [United Kingdom and other countries](https://beaconbio.org/en/report/?reportid=65d8c4f1-e15b-4d3c-8681-f6d10b58c292&utm) in Europe and central Asia in early 2026.

These losses of status are no mystery. Measles is [one of the most contagious diseases](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/causes/index.html) and still [circulates in much of the world](https://theconversation.com/why-millions-of-people-around-the-world-are-contracting-measles-in-2026-289667). What keeps the disease in check is [herd immunity](https://theconversation.com/what-is-herd-immunity-a-public-health-expert-and-a-medical-laboratory-scientist-explain-170520) – when a high enough percentage of the population is vaccinated to break the chains of transmission. For measles, that’s [at least 95%](https://www.cdc.gov/global-measles-vaccination/about/index.html). But in 2025-26, only 92% of kindergartners in the U.S. [received the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine](https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html).

I’m an [epidemiologist who studies misinformation](https://publichealth.uic.edu/profiles/wallace-katrine/) in the same way others study smoking or air pollution: as an exposure that makes populations sick. For years I’ve watched [vaccine misinformation help erode the coverage](https://theconversation.com/vaccine-misinformation-distorts-science-a-biochemist-explains-how-rfk-jr-and-his-lawyers-claims-threaten-public-health-246000) that kept measles from spreading.

**An Effective Vaccine**

A measles vaccine has [existed in the U.S. since 1963](https://theconversation.com/rfk-jr-wants-to-scrutinize-the-vaccine-schedule-but-its-safety-record-is-already-decades-long-271408). The combined MMR vaccine followed in 1971; two doses are about [97% effective](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/vaccines/index.html). A federal program created in 1993 made it [free for eligible children](https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines-for-children/about/index.html). After widespread vaccination efforts, reported cases [dropped more than 99%](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00053391.htm), and by 2000 measles was [declared eliminated](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html).

But due to the success of the MMR vaccine, within a generation most parents and many doctors had never even seen a measles case. The experts who certified elimination in 2000 warned that [maintaining elimination status would require](https://doi.org/10.1086/377696) sustained high rates of vaccination, fast outbreak response and strong surveillance. Drop any one of these conditions and imported cases would spread.

[Video 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dG_ULyeN5d0)

So how does a country with a 97% effective vaccine lose measles elimination status? One obvious explanation: The vaccine worked so well that people forgot what the disease does.

[Before the vaccine](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/about/history.html), measles infected 3 million to 4 million Americans a year. Tens of thousands were hospitalized, and hundreds died. Parents didn’t need convincing. They had seen it. Even with most cases unreported, the [official count in 1963 was nearly 400,000 cases](https://abcnews.com/Health/history-measles-cases-us-meeting-decide-elimination-status/story?id=138042017).

About [1 in 20 children](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/signs-symptoms/index.html) who contract measles develop pneumonia. The virus can also erase part of the immune system’s memory, an effect called [immune amnesia](https://theconversation.com/measles-can-ravage-the-immune-system-and-brain-causing-long-term-damage-a-virologist-explains-252354), leaving children open to infections they had already beaten.

In rare cases, it causes a fatal brain disease, [subacute sclerosing panencephalitis](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560673/), which appears years after apparent recovery. In 2025, a [child in Los Angeles died of it](https://www.idse.net/Pediatric-Infections/Article/09-25/California-SSPE-Measles-Death/78258).

**A Surge of Outbreaks—And Deaths**

As of Nov. 12, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention counted [5,412 cases for 2026](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html) – the highest number since 1991 – and 591 hospitalizations. Among children under 5, [1 in 6 have been hospitalized](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html).

[Six deaths](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html) appear in the CDC’s 2026 count, which [now relies](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/measles/cdc-s-new-tracking-method-measles-deaths-puzzles-experts) on federal death certificate data. States, using a broader definition, report a total of 10 deaths: seven in [Pennsylvania](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles), one in [New York](https://www.health.ny.gov/diseases/communicable/measles/data.htm) and two in [Wisconsin](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/immunization/measles.htm).

[Pennsylvania’s outbreak](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles) alone has produced 1,542 cases and 305 hospitalizations, by the state’s Nov. 13 count. [Major outbreaks](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html) have also hit South Carolina, Utah and Arizona since the West Texas outbreak of early 2025, which was the start of the national surge of measles outbreaks. [Utah’s outbreak](https://files.epi.utah.gov/Utah%20measles%20dashboard.html), which began in June 2025, has gone well past the 12-month mark. That outbreak alone breaches the WHO’s definition of measles elimination and could have [triggered the loss of elimination status](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6041119/us-measles-elimination-status-vaccines-cdc-paho).

**Fertile Ground for Misinformation**

When no one remembers the disease, the vaccine becomes the only thing left to fear. Misinformation feeds on that imbalance.

Parents who had never seen measles had [nothing vivid to weigh](https://doi.org/10.1001/virtualmentor.2012.14.1.fred1-1201) against claims of vaccine risk, so even discredited risks felt plausible. A 1998 paper [fraudulently linking MMR to autism](https://doi.org/10.4103/0019-5545.82529) was [retracted in 2010](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.c696), and its author [lost his medical license](https://www.theguardian.com/society/2010/may/24/andrew-wakefield-struck-off-gmc). But the damage was already done, and this myth [persists to this day](https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/kff-polling-on-health-information-and-trust/?entry=false-or-unproven-health-claims-belief-in-false-or-unproven-health-claims), even though studies that included [millions of children have found no link](https://www.chop.edu/vaccine-education-center/vaccine-safety/vaccines-and-other-conditions/autism).

During the COVID-19 pandemic, [vaccine misinformation proliferated](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0263746) in echo chambers on social media. It is no surprise that the percentage of kindergartners who have received their MMR shots [has fallen every year](https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html) since the 2019-20 school year.

In a 2025 KFF poll, parents who believed any false measles claim were more than [twice as likely to have skipped or delayed vaccines](https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/kff-tracking-poll-on-health-information-and-trust-update-on-common-vaccine-myths/). Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the anti-vaccine movement has also used the banner of [medical freedom](https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI149072) to gain a larger, more [mainstream audience](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/31/opinion/anti-vaccine-movement.html).

**Federal Policy Fuels Further Confusion**

Now these arguments have found an audience in federal policy.

On Aug. 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed an order calling for [MMR to be split into three single-disease shots](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/08/delivering-gold-standard-childhood-vaccine-recommendations-for-americans/), which are [not sold in the United States](https://theconversation.com/executive-order-on-vaccines-bypasses-an-evidence-based-process-that-has-kept-kids-safe-289469). There is [no published evidence](https://perma.cc/W2VE-P3YQ) that separating MMR offers any benefit, and more doctor visits mean [more chances for missed doses](https://doi.org/10.1080/21645515.2017.1362515).

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested in August that [Pennsylvania’s first two measles-associated deaths](https://theconversation.com/cdc-vs-pennsylvania-why-conflicting-public-health-messages-jeopardize-public-safety-291239) “may even have been altogether fabricated.” State officials had investigated both. While [questioning the vaccine](https://www.factcheck.org/2026/05/a-timeline-of-rfk-jr-s-mixed-messaging-on-the-measles-vaccine/) and measles deaths, he has promoted [vitamin A and nutrition](https://abcnews.com/Health/rfk-jr-claims-measles-treated-vitamin-linked-poor/story?id=119713193) as measles cures. The CDC classifies vitamin A as a [supportive treatment](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html#cdc_clinical_overview_treat_pat-patient-management), not a cure or vaccine substitute.

Vaccination rates for the MMR vaccine among U.S. kindergartners [fell from 95.2% in 2019-20 to 92.4% in 2025-26](https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html). Exemptions from any required vaccine rose to a [record 4.2%](https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html).

Of this year’s cases, [96% were unvaccinated or of unknown](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html) status. The [92.4% kindergarten vaccination rate](https://www.cdc.gov/schoolvaxview/data/index.html) leaves about 280,000 kindergartners without documented MMR. Among states, Idaho has the lowest MMR rate with [75.2% among Idaho kindergartners](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/ivac/resources/reports/monitoring-childhood-immunization-at-the-state-level/idaho#coverage), while some counties and communities there and elsewhere have even lower rates.

[Adult immunity also has gaps](https://www.cdc.gov/measles/data-research/index.html): Adults are 41% of this year’s cases, and 15% of them were hospitalized. Many who were vaccinated before 1989, when a second MMR dose was added, got only one.

**Roadblocks to Recovery**

Regaining elimination status means the U.S experiencing at least [12 months without continuous transmission](https://doi.org/10.1086/381556). That will require the same factors that led to the U.S. earning that status in 2000: stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates.

But it will also require federal health leadership that is focused on bringing those things about.

The Department of Health and Human Services [blames current vaccination gaps](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/measles/hearings-rfk-jr-claims-no-responsibility-measles-spread) on missed pediatrician appointments during the COVID-19 pandemic. [CDC Director Erica Schwartz](https://theconversation.com/the-cdc-has-a-new-director-now-comes-the-hard-part-289677) said that the agency would [not make any changes](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/10/health/cdc-measles-elimination-response) in measles response efforts in light of losing elimination status.

Additionally, [orders like August’s](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/08/delivering-gold-standard-childhood-vaccine-recommendations-for-americans/) about the MMR vaccine, and [revisions to long-standing vaccine recommendations](https://theconversation.com/federal-judge-temporarily-blocks-rfk-jr-s-vaccine-agenda-an-epidemiologist-answers-questions-parents-may-have-278709), are [weakening vaccination efforts](https://www.networkforphl.org/resources/federal-and-state-attacks-on-vaccine-policy/).

Also, on top of a [chronically underfunded public health infrastructure](https://ourpublicservice.org/know-the-facts/resource-library/reports/the-cost-of-cutting-american-science-how-federal-cuts-diminish-public-health-capacity) , many career public health scientists [lost their jobs](https://www.npr.org/sections/shots-health-news/2025/03/27/nx-s1-5342414/hhs-doge-rif-rfk-job-cuts) in 2025. The surveillance capacity that made elimination possible [has been substantially weakened](https://theconversation.com/how-cuts-to-cdc-are-dismantling-its-capacity-to-protect-americans-health-284280).

So what does this mean for Americans? The loss of measles elimination status in the U.S. does not change the fact that the vaccine is safe and effective – and it is now more important than ever. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: There is Still Time to Stall the AI Apocalypse
content:
Who hasn’t worried of late that the AI apocalypse is nigh? Just in the past few days, air traffic control, banking, communication, security or other network systems in the United States and around the world have gone down, stoking [fears](https://x.com/nicoleperlroth/status/2122763662796689668) of AI-powered cyberattacks.

Such fears really took off in September, when many AI insiders began sounding the doomsday alarm, following incidents in which AI agents acted in ways that their human handlers hadn’t intended, such as the Hugging Face attack. The CEOs of the major frontier AI companies Anthropic and Open AI quickly [called for regulation](https://nautil.us/ai-engineers-are-having-their-oppenheimer-destroyer-of-worlds-moment-1284956) to “pace the frontier,” or slow the training of new AI models, so that safety measures could catch up.

**Read more: “**[**Isaac Asimov Showed Us How to Avoid the AI Apocalypse**](https://nautil.us/isaac-asimov-showed-us-how-to-avoid-the-ai-apocalypse-1285249)**”**

It wasn’t the first time that insiders had urged caution in the face of super rapid development. An open [letter](https://futureoflife.org/open-letter/pause-giant-ai-experiments/) in March of 2023 signed by more than 1,000 researchers and technology experts called on all AI labs to “immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of systems more powerful than GPT-4.”

So far, the governments of the United States and China, home to the major players in the AI race, have refused to slow AI through regulation, and few private solutions have been proposed that seem to match the scale of the worry. But one new proposal on the table would hardwire a 10-year pause on training new models into the technology itself.

In early October, more than two dozen researchers from The University of California, Berkeley, Stanford, Oxford, and other universities and institutions in the U.S., the United Kingdom, and Canada published a [working paper](https://hardwired-pause.ai/paper) that proposed mandating the use of a special kind of chip, called an inference-only chip, that can only be used for existing AI models and has no training capability.

The authors of the report argue that because of the scale of the infrastructure required to train AI models, and the near-monopoly that many of major chip supply chain players have, it’s a solution that could have legs.

I spoke with co-authors William Fithian, a statistics professor, and Wesley Holliday, a philosophy professor, both from UC Berkeley, about how their hardwired pause would be enforced, why it would not crash the U.S. economy, what such an effort might have in common with nuclear arms race controls, and how data center bans might help.  
******In early October, you published a**[**paper**](https://hardwired-pause.ai/)**that proposed a strategy for pausing the development of frontier models, one that you called “hardwired.” Can you tell me how this proposal would work?**

**Holliday:** It’s a template that you can specialize in different ways, but it entails a temporary but durable stop on training associated with OpenAI and Anthropic and the other frontier developers for maybe 10 years. Getting there involves stopping the production of AI chips that are capable of training new frontier models. We call those “training-capable” AI chips, the kind of chips that Nvidia makes that are in these massive data centers, like the Stargate facility in Texas that was used to train GPT-6 Astra.

During the pause, you stop producing training-capable chips, and instead, you produce what we call inference-only chips, which allow you to use existing models. When you type in a question, the AI model can do what’s called inference to answer your question. And that can be done on these inference-only chips very efficiently, in fact. But the inference-only chips would not be practically useful for training new models. Even if you had a lot of these inference-only chips, they would not allow you to efficiently train GPT-6.5 and so on.

**What makes these chips different?**

**Holliday:** The key point is there are certain operations that you need to do on a chip in order to train a new model. And the inference-only chip restricts the ability to perform those operations. Instead, it specializes on the operations that are needed for inference. In fact, you could set them up so that they only run approved models that have passed some safety standards. These chips would prevent training new models whether it’s a human doing it or the previous model doing it, so recursive self-improvement through training of new models wouldn’t be feasible on inference-only chips.

**How would this be enforced? What would stop a well-resourced actor from defeating it or getting around it?**

**Fithian:** The main thing to know is that AI chips are produced using one of the most complex, sophisticated, and concentrated supply chains that has ever existed. There’s one company in the Netherlands that makes all of the extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which basically print these chips. The number of vendors is fairly small. There’s one company in Germany that makes all of the very high-precision optics, the mirrors required for these lithography machines. And there are a number of other components or parts of the process that are near monopolies.

Indigenizing the supply chain, having all aspects of the supply chain within one country, is extremely difficult. China has been trying to do this, and has probably come the closest, because they’ve been shut out of various parts of the chip supply chain by the U.S. and Western order. But they still haven’t really come that close to fully indigenizing their supply chain. They are able to build the second-best type of lithography machines, but they still need to get other components from overseas. Basically, a handful of governments really can choke off and govern the supply of new chips.

Then there are other things that you would need to enforce. Because it would take time to produce these inference-only chips. You need a plan to govern the existing training-capable chips in the meantime. A lot of work has been done actually on tools for verifying that training-capable chips are not doing training. You can verify that they’re set up in a way that would make it hard for them to do training. You also need to make sure that you find and register the vast majority of the chips. But these are very expensive capital goods, so they leave massive paper trails when they’re manufactured, when they’re sold, written off on taxes. If you buy $10 million worth of computer equipment, you definitely tell the IRS about it if you’re a business. So they all have paper trails a mile long. If you don’t tell the IRS, then you lose massive tax savings, so you have very high compliance. But to back up, any discussion of the effectiveness of verification has to start by asking what is the scale of violation that you would need to worry about?

In this case, the answer is very favorable. To train GPT-6 Astra, it took probably four to six months using more than 100,000 chips at this data center Wes mentioned, called Stargate, that’s larger than Central Park. This is something that’s very hard to do while you’re pretending to use all of your chips for some other activity. It’s less like breaking into the _Louvre_ and stealing the _Mona Lisa_ and more like taking the entire Renaissance collection.

That’s good news because the verification tools are still being developed, and it’ll probably take some time before they’re really solid. By the way, the entire country of China has less hardware than OpenAI does. It would be very difficult for people to cheat at the scale that would be required to actually advance the AI frontier.

**Would this hardwired pause work then without China’s participation?**

**Holliday:** We only study a plan where the U.S. and China both want to pause, provided they can be confident that the other side is pausing. That being said, the U.S. could unilaterally pause for some period of time, and that might encourage China to get interested in a pause. But the plan that we study in the paper, to get the full 10 years, we imagine that both the U.S. and China are parties to the agreement, hopefully other states as well.

**And you would need China and the U.S. to agree, I’m assuming, because even if countries like Germany and the Netherlands decided that they weren’t going to allow these major supply chain companies to provide the technology necessary for the chips, China and the U.S. could just indigenize that production capacity?**

**Fithian:** It’s certainly possible that they could. I think it would be very hard to do covertly if the intelligence communities of both countries were very intent on detecting any such thing. But if either country hadn’t agreed to pause, and they were determined to overtly keep on scaling up their AI industry, then they could at least be slowed down a lot. But it would be much more difficult to impose a pause on a world superpower than for them to agree. Just to be clear, we consider a scenario where they come to believe that it’s in their interest to pause. But we don’t assume that they love each other or that they trust each other.

It’s got to be verified. We assume that their desire to pause is only conditional on their ability to verify that the other state is pausing. It’s hard to make a deal if you can’t prove to your counterparty that you’re keeping the deal yourself. That’s why this verification technology is so important. It’ll allow countries to make deals, because it gives them the power to demonstrate compliance.

**What is the hardest part of making this hardwired pause idea work?**

**Holliday:** Possibly just the political willingness to do it, although things are changing so fast. Even the political willingness may change in the coming months, depending on the level of disruption to our society that AI causes.

**When you say things are changing so fast, what do you mean?**

**Holliday:** AI capabilities are rapidly increasing. We’re seeing all these cyberattacks, some of which have been directly attributed to AI. In other cases, people are wondering, “Is this due to AI enabled cybercrime?” If that were to really escalate to the point of crippling some critical infrastructure, then what policymakers consider reasonable options might change rapidly.

**Fithian:** Even in the current environment, in recent months, we’ve seen a lot of people calling for pauses, including a number of American lawmakers and political figures, such as Bernie Sanders, Abdul El-Sayed, Elizabeth Warren, and representatives in the House. Former national security adviser Susan Rice has been very vocal in calling for a pause. But also some Republicans, like Peggy Noonan, a former speechwriter for President Reagan, have called for a pause, as have a fair number of experts, most prominently, Yoshua Bengio, chair of the International AI Safety Report and co-chair of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.

**You argue in the paper that a pause on AI development would not crash the economy. Why not?**

**Holliday:** The current models, if they were to diffuse throughout businesses, would already give productivity a big boost. They’re already good enough for many, many business tasks. They’re just not as widely employed as they could be. In addition, our plan allows people to keep scaling up inference, building these inference-only chips, inference-only data centers, and so on. We would just be scaling it in a different direction, letting people use the existing technology more widely rather than creating ever more powerful models.

**Fithian:** In some ways, you’d also redirect more effort toward things like using current models to do medical research, to build products for customers, and so on. Right now, a lot of the talent that would otherwise be working on those things is just working on making the models better and better, rather than trying to use the abilities that we already have.

**There are clearly some historical precedents for this kind of coordinated international pause on technological and scientific advances, and you mention a couple of them in the paper itself: controlling military uses of nuclear energy and promoting peaceful ones, for example. What is different this time, and what do you think we can learn from those examples?**

**Holliday:** The nuclear case is an interesting analogy, but it also has some disanalogies. An analogy is that in both cases, you need to keep track of hardware. In our case, it’s things like not only the AI chips themselves, but the giant lithography machines that we talked about. In both cases, you also have the difficulty of producing the physical item. In fact, it might even be more difficult to produce the AI chips than it is to produce enriched uranium for nuclear weapons. So there’s an analogy in the fact that you have to worry about these physical items.

But there are some disanalogies. One of them is that private companies are the ones that are advancing the AI frontier as opposed to governments advancing military uses of nuclear weapons. Another one, which Will likes to point out, which I think is very good, is that people didn’t really worry about the nukes going rogue and taking actions on their own. The kind of loss of control risks that we saw in the Hugging Face incident were not as much of a concern in the case of nuclear weapons. In other incidents, you saw OpenAI models even hacking other governments’ websites. Imagine if the nukes in our silos could take it upon themselves to launch at other countries.

But what they have in common with almost all international agreements is that clearly, all states have a common interest in maintaining human control over artificial intelligence, making sure that human workers have things to do and are provided for, preventing too much social disruption.

**Fithian:** And preventing the kinds of cyberattacks that we’re seeing and possible bioattacks that many people are worried we could see.

**Is there any possibility that it’s already just too late?**

**Fithian:** It can always get worse. Even if right now we have more disruption than we would like, we could still have tremendously more disruption to our society. So it might be prudent to pause now and see whether we can manage the existing risks before exacerbating them. But it’s a critical question, and one of the really concerning things about AI risk is that we don’t know when we’ve crossed certain thresholds. We know that the open-weight models we have now, from which people have removed the safeguards, are very capable at doing cyberattacks. As far as we know, they’re not capable of effectively designing novel pathogens, but it’s really hard to be sure, because they just haven’t been around for very long. It would probably be unwise to wait until the last minute to stop, until we’re sure that we’ve crossed a threshold.

But what’s difficult is to keep track of what people are doing with the models that already exist. Running the current models is much cheaper than training a new one. Even if governments don’t want to pause, they’re going to need to have a plan for controlling the hardware. We’re not going to want terrorist groups and criminal organizations and rogue states to be able to run the most advanced models, even if we were to make the choice to keep on developing them. I think we’re already past the point where it’s acceptable for just anyone in the world to be able to run the most powerful models without safeguards.

**You mentioned earlier as a disanalogy with nuclear arms race controls the fact that these models and technologies are being built by private companies instead of research institutions or governments. And of course, they’re not just private companies, but hugely powerful companies with tons of investors and money and political might behind them. How does that change what can realistically be achieved?**

**Fithian:** That’s true. And they get more powerful every day as well. People talk about coordination games and prisoner’s dilemmas. People like to bring up game theory in the case of AI. And one thing that’s true when you have a lot of private companies is that it’s very hard for them to coordinate, even now when the leading companies at least are asking governments to regulate them. It’s hard for them to coordinate with each other, and even if they did, then other companies would compete with them and so on. You see it in the game theory, but it also makes logical sense, that it’s harder for a large number of players to coordinate than just two players.

If you just have the United States and China, it’s easier for them to come to an agreement. There’s always going to be fear. You have to address the fear with verification. But it is easier to have a deal because you have two hopefully rational agents coming together and talking about what to do. Still, the power of these AI companies is very concerning, and I think the more powerful the models get, the more worried I get about it. When I got my ballot and I saw all the many initiatives to vote on in California, I realized I needed to start educating myself about them. Of course, my first instinct is, “Oh, maybe I should ask Claude about them.” But then I stopped myself because that’s not how I want democratic decisions to be made. I don’t know how many other people would have stopped themselves. And of course, instead of using Claude, I just used Google search instead.

**How important is data center capacity to frontier training? Could data center bans or bottlenecks in the U.S. slow frontier training capacity significantly?**

**Holliday:** One thing we discuss in the report is how the most concerning economic issue is the way this data center buildout is highly leveraged, and the debt financing is using various tricks to obfuscate where the risk lies. Regulators definitely should be concerned about that, regardless of whether there is a pause.

**Fithian:** It strikes me that it could be financially stabilizing, actually if the bottleneck for building a billion new data centers is getting the permit from the local government rather than just how much more can you leverage your financial investment.

**How much of new training capacity is dependent on new data center buildouts versus what’s already there?**

**Holliday:**To make their plans over the next several years, they need a big build up. The question is just where is it going to happen? If there are data center bans in the U.S., they will try to build those data centers elsewhere. But for sure, they need to scale up the data centers massively in order to meet their multi-year plans.

**Fithian:** Yeah, that’s right. Basically, every couple of years they’ve got roughly 10 times as much compute as they had before, literally. That’s why what Wes mentioned about not making more training-capable hardware can actually be so effective. If we stopped two years ago, we’d have 10 times less hardware than we have now. The scaling of the models just physically could not have continued. I’m sure the models would’ve still gotten somewhat better, but most of the compute that companies would be using to train the models of 2028 hasn’t been built yet. If we don’t make it, that step alone makes it a lot harder to scale the model. Of course, a data center bottleneck also helps with verification because if you’re trying to govern a smaller number of chips, then it’s easier and you have more margin for error. But we wouldn’t rely solely on not making more training chips.

**Is anyone making inference-only chips now?**

**Holliday:** Great question. There’s been a move in the last few years toward chips that are specialized for inference. You might call them inference-optimized or inference-specialized chips. Because there’s so much demand for inference, why not make chips that are specially designed for inference? Whether those chips count as inference-only, that’s a higher bar. But certainly things are trending in the right direction there.

There’s a Canadian company called Taalas that was acquired by AMD that got rather far in the pure-inference direction. They hardwire a particular AI model onto the chip so you can only run that model on the chip. It’s like a CD-ROM, where the weights and architecture are burned into the chip. They were just doing that purely for economic reasons because those chips are extremely fast and low energy consumption. That’s why they were developing them. But a version of that style of chip could be what we would call an inference-only chip for the purposes of the hardwired pause. And that’s not the only type of inference-only chip that one can make. In fact, at Berkeley, we’re starting a project to work on the design of these inference-only chips. I’ve heard rumors of other people starting new companies to work on inference-only chips.

**What would need to happen next to make this hardwired pause idea a reality?**

**Holliday:** There are two things that people can do right away. One is the idea that we discussed in the paper about a global chip census. We need to know where the existing training-capable chips are. Organizations and governments should get the ball rolling on understanding how to do that, how to find out where the training-capable chips are.

The other thing that people can do right now—nobody needs to wait for governments—is start developing these inference-only chips or the verification technology for training-capable chips. Will mentioned that during some period of time before the inference-only chips are widely available, we’re going to need to keep using training-capable chips to serve customers. During that period, we’re going to have to use so-called verification methods to make sure that those training-capable chips are not doing new training runs. We’re going to need so-called sociotechnical solutions to reduce the likelihood of somebody doing a training run covertly.

**Fithian:** There has actually been a lot of work on this verification technology. That’s not at the brainstorming stage. But there’s more we can do. We don’t need to wait for a grand international bargain. In fact, greater development in the verification and inference-only chip technologies will facilitate the grand international bargain.

**Holliday:** Right. And as Will said, there’s already a large verification community, a large body of work on verification, but there are a lot of questions that people are still making progress on. The faster they can make progress, the better. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# The AI Forecasting Agenda

### ...

[![Image 2: Scott Alexander's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!HTBd!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7b500d22-1176-42ad-afaa-5d72bc36a809_44x44.png)](https://substack.com/@astralcodexten)
